methodology.nativeConfiguration: One native front at a time plus a fixed pristine native origin; daemon off and master_process off for both
methodology.transport: Loopback HTTP/1.1, keepalive, closed loop, one outstanding request per client lane, no pipelining
methodology.workload: Static file sendfile on and native reverse proxy, exact 1024-byte response verified for every completed request
methodology.order: For every workload/concurrency pair: even repetition baseline then candidate; odd repetition candidate then baseline
methodology.timing: A separate C-client warmup primes native caches/pools; measured client uses fresh connections and drains admitted requests; throughput denominator includes connection setup and drain
methodology.latency: C-client full-response durations; log2-microsecond histogram quantile upper bounds, no cross-sample pooled quantiles
methodology.resources: Linux /proc front/origin CPU ticks; RSS sampled every25ms, not true peak; C client self CPU/maxRSS; separate Node orchestration CPU

limitations: Synthetic short local smoke comparison; no confidence interval, regression threshold or global speedup claim.
C client, native front and native origin still share a host and can limit each other; no open-loop or remote generator.
Host scheduling and other workloads are uncontrolled; balanced order reduces but does not remove noise.
Single-process master-off execution does not measure production multiworker scaling, reloads, TLS, HTTP2/3, QUIC, mail or disk-cold workloads.
Native CPU uses discrete scheduler ticks; its snapshot window includes client process creation/exit around traffic. RSS sampling can miss peaks; C maxRSS is process-lifetime high water.
The candidate QUIC parser fix is not exercised by these HTTP1 workloads. Ratios are observations, not evidence that the fix speeds these workloads up.
